content.content:
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as

No, your ruling is not the problem. The review says the opposite: unboxed `double[]` and sizes in the type are the specification's own shape, and the team left breadcrumbs pointing that way. Both stand.

The main contradiction is between the model's text and the compiler's checker. C4 runs on the interpreter, which dispatches at run time, so its vocabulary got away with unsized arrays: every view returns a plain `Array`, and `x DOT x` works only because the interpreter finds the vector version at run time. The compile path resolves types statically and refuses that. The reviewer proved it with a probe: the same line passes on the interpreter and is refused by the checker. So the first compiled microGPT fails in `FlatArrays.fss` before any array is ever built, and the design never says so.

That is exactly your "sizes are a central design point" ruling coming home. The decision it forces, D in the review: either the sizes go into the model's own text, which is the specification's shape and changes model lines, diff shown to you first, or the vocabulary is declared over unsized arrays, model unchanged, and there is no static shape check.

Two more decisions carry weight:
- How `double[]` gets under the generic array. The design's default, a factory choosing the store at run time, is refused by the checker. The routes left are both Java: specialising in the class loader, the team's own direction, or one storing object per element type.
- Which library. The design says "into the compiler's prelude", which means the standard library written twice. The alternative is one library serving both worlds, which needs the 92 tower errors classified first. No default there.

The rest is order and safety: no stop conditions, natives-first measured to buy nothing, and the "unconstrained size becomes 0" default is the unsafe side.

1:<!-- The design sketch for the first reserved fork of PLAN.md, the array representation on the compile path, written 2026-09-19 by a worker for Pavol. It assembles what next-climb.md §3a said a sketch must hold: what exists on both paths, what microGPT needs, the options with their costs, what the specification and the team's drafts say, and a decision tree. Three compile probes were run in a private cache (§8); no tracked file was changed and nothing was committed but this file. Every recommendation is labelled "default" and decides nothing. One line per paragraph. -->
2:
3:# How arrays should be built in the compiled world
4:
5:## 0. The words used below
6:
7:Boxing: a number wrapped in a heap object so that it can be treated like any other object. On the compile path every `RR64` is an `FRR64`, a Java object with one `double` field (`compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64.java:14-19`); adding two of them allocates a third. "Unboxed" means the bare JVM `double`, which lives in a register or in a `double[]` and costs nothing to make.
8:
9:Stamping: the compiler writes a generic declaration (`Box[\T\]`) once as a template class; when a program first uses `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader reads the template and rewrites it with the argument's name filled in (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`, the general case at `:210-290`; `Instantiater.java:48` substitutes the names). One stamped class per distinct argument list.
10:
11:`nat` parameter: a static parameter that is a natural number rather than a type, written `Vector[\T, nat s0\]`; it puts a size into the type so that `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` times `Matrix[\T,m,p\]` can be declared with the shared `m`.
12:
13:Descriptor: the JVM's spelling of a type in bytecode. `D` is a bare double, `[D` an array of doubles, `Lcom/sun/…/FRR64;` a reference to the boxed class. Whether a field is boxed or not is exactly which of these its descriptor is.
14:
15:View: an object that implements the array protocol (`get`/`put`) over some other array's storage without copying, such as a row of a matrix or a transposed matrix.
16:
17:Rank: the number of indices an array takes; a vector has rank 1, a matrix rank 2, `Array3` rank 3.
18:
19:Project units: a rung is one worker session plus one skeptic under the batch script (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`); batch 1 was four rungs, fifteen agents, 3 h 11 min, with the full gate run once at 830 s (FACTS, ladder section). A rung that touches a `.java` or `.scala` file forces the full gate pair; a library-only rung may drop `ant testSystem` (`next-climb.md` §5). The regression net is the ladder's 85 passing files (`compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt`).
20:
21:## 1. What an array is in the interpreter today
22:
23:An array is a trait, not a primitive. `Array[\E,I\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1322`) is generic in the element type `E` and the index type `I` (`ZZ32` for rank 1, `(ZZ32,ZZ32)` for rank 2) and carries no size in its type. Its protocol is `get(i)` and `put(i, v)`; subscripting is sugar for them (`opr[i:I]:=(v:E) = put(offset(i),v)`, `FortressLibrary.fss:1886-1889`). `ReadableArray` (`.fsi:1247`) is the read half; `Indexed` (`.fsi:1111`) makes every array a generator, so `for x <- a` and `BIG +` work over it.
24:
25:Sizes enter one layer up. `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]` (`.fsi:1435`), `Array2` (`.fss:2289`) and `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2\]` (`.fsi:1652`) put the lower bound and size of each dimension into the type. `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` (`.fsi:1460`) is an `Array1` that is also an additive group (`+`, `-`, unary `-`, `zero`, plus `scale`, `pmul`, `dot`); `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` (`.fsi:1578`) is an `Array2` with `mul[\nat s2\]`, `rmul`, `lmul`, `t()`. Both exclude the multiplicative ring because juxtaposition is the inner product (FACT
26:
27:Storage is one object per rank-1 array, holding boxed values. `PrimitiveArray[\T, nat s0\]` (`LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:15-27`) binds `get`, `put` and `init0` to Java glue; the glue allocates an `AtomicArray` of the evaluator's boxed `FValue`s (`interpreter/glue/prim/PrimitiveArray.java:35, 44-56`; `evaluator/transactions/AtomicArray.java:23`). A rank-2 array is a rank-1 array with the index folded as `i s1 + j`, row by row (`__DefaultArray2`, `FortressLibrary.fss:2415-2421`); rank 3 the same. So the interpreter's arrays are already flat, row-major storage under a trait; what they are 
28:
29:The everyday operations are Fortress loops over `get`/`put`. `fill(f)` is `for i <- zeroIndices() do init0(i, f(toIndex(i))) end` (`.fss:1974-1976`); `map(f)` and `ivmap(f)` (map with the index) make a `replica` of the same shape and `fill` it (`.fss:2135-2138`); `t()` returns a transposed view, not a copy (`.fss:2395` for `Array2`, `:2559` for `Matrix`). The whole protocol runs from `trait Indexed` at `.fss:1636` to the end of `SubArray3` at `:2808`, about 1,170 lines, plus the 54 lines of `NativeArray.fss` and the integer-only scalar extension at `.fss:4477-4517`.
30:
31:A run-time size becomes a type by reflection. `array[\E\](x: ZZ32)` (`.fss:1922`) calls `reflect(x)`, which returns a value of type `N[\n\]` with the number baked into the nat (`LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`), and `__arr1[\E, nat n\](…, x: N[\n\])` (`.fss:1930`) then builds an `Array1[\E,0,n\]`. The interpreter can do this because a nat is a type in its own lattice, made at run time (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java`).
32:
33:A nat is checked at run time, at dispatch, and only then. When a call meets a nat parameter, a literal must be equal and a symbol is bound (`IntNat.unifyStaticArg`, `IntNat.java:127-147`); a mismatch is "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (FACTS, execution model, last bullet). Nothing is optimised on a nat anywhere.
34:
35:## 2. What the compiled world has
36:
37:The compiler's own library is small: `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` 778 lines with a 1,627-line body, `CompilerLibrary.fsi` 356 with 718. It has no `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` or `Matrix` with a body. The one `nat` declaration in it is `trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\] extends Object end` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:279`), empty.
38:
39:It has exactly one numeric array, and it is the shape the 2012 team chose for this world. `trait ZZ32Vector` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:555-572`) has no static parameters at all: `shape`, `nrows`, `ncols`, `copy`, `opr[i]`, `opr[i,j]`, their `:=` forms, `|self|`, `fill`, `fill2`. Its body (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:1101-1136`) forwards every member to Java helpers imported at `.fss:299-305`. The Java class `FZZ32Vector` holds an unboxed `int[]` and four shape integers (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java:18-19`); a 2-D index is folded to `(i-lower_x)*dim_y + (j-lower_y)` (`:65`); 
40:
100:
101:On storage: "As in Fortran, Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), with the note that distributions and `HeapSequence` "are not yet supported" (`:15-16`). Nothing in the prose says boxed or unboxed; the intent is an array as a structure over a linear store, which both (b) and (c) are.
102:
103:On sizes in types: "types can be parametric with respect to other types and values (most notably natural numbers)" (`preliminaries/intro/nutshell.tex:85-86`); a nat parameter's semantics is "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values" (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:82`), and the chapter opens with "Non-type static parameters and static expressions are not yet supported" (`:15-17`). The internal meeting record's one implementation stance is "don't instantiate" (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`, §a).
104:
105:On the intended aggregate: "Guy's proposal for making tensors the principal user-level indexed aggregate type in Fortress (06/27/07)" and his email "Arrays, matrices, and tensors (short)" of 12/15/06 (`appendices/future.tex:63-65`); the FAQ's answer to variable-sized arrays with static bounds checking is a link to a wiki page that no longer exists (`appendices/FAQ.tex:55-57`); the emails themselves are not in the repository (`map/design-intent-sources.md:111, 128`).
106:
107:On the compiled encoding: the JVM paper says "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds in domain and range" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`), which is why stamping is a renaming, and that the template's side file "contains info about the static parameters, including their names, whether they are types, oprs, or nats" (`:142`), so nats were meant to travel through the template machinery by name. The team's own unboxing note is `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:18-30`: four cases, "primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean", singleton objects, unb
108:
109:The drafts say nothing about arrays. `Library/incomplete/` (24 files) contains no mention of an array. `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (783 lines, imported by nothing) are the generator and reduction protocol, `Container`, `DefaultGeneratorImplementation`, without `Indexed` or any array. `Fortress.Operators.fsi.INCOMPLETE` is the algebra above `Number` and names no aggregate. What the team shipped in this world is `ZZ32Vector`, and it is the only precedent with code behind it.
110:
111:## 6. The decision tree
112:
113:Question 1. Is the storage of an `RR64` array a bare `double[]` (unboxed) or an array of boxed objects?
114:Branch "boxed": option (a); the kernels compile soonest; the 6.3-6.5× stays; making it fast later means a second storage class and second natives under the same traits.
115:Branch "unboxed": options (b) and (c); the `RR64` array is a hand-written class on the `ZZ32Vector` pattern, never a stamped generic; boxed traffic at the trait boundary until either natives or the code generator remove it.
116:Default: unboxed. This is the order on record ("unboxing designed into the first", `POSITIONS.md:14`) and the probe shows a stamped generic cannot get there later by itself.
117:
118:Question 2. Is the unboxed class hidden behind the generic `Array[\T,I\]` that the model names, or is it its own type?
119:Branch "own type", option (b): no `Array`/`Vector`/`Matrix` names in the compiler world; nothing in microGPT or on the ladder moves; the model is respelled to the new names, against the position that the model's text is the notation.
120:Branch "behind the generic", option (c): the model's `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` resolves as written; the boxed default object serves every other element type and the ladder's files; the specialised object is chosen by the factory.
121:Default: behind the generic, with the vocabulary's own `vec`/`mat` constructors making the `RR64` object directly; the type-tag factory is a later convenience.
122:
123:Question 3. Where do the loops run unboxed?
124:Branch "inside native whole-array operations": Java helpers over `double[]` for the contractions and elementwise maps; a box per operation; no code-generator change; user lambdas still box per element.
125:Branch "in generated code": the code generator learns `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` for statically `RR64` code; every rung `.java` under the full gate; unlocks unboxed loops written in Fortress.
126:Default: natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4, once the measured residue says what it is worth.
127:
128:Question 4. Where do sizes live?
129:Branch "in the type now": every sized declaration waits on the nat fork; run-time sizes need a compile-world `reflect` that does not exist.
130:Branch "run-time fields only": the `ZZ32Vector` shape; the spec's sizes-in-types intent is dropped, and the model's 20 nat-carrying declarations are respelled.
131:Branch "layered": the storage carries sizes as fields; `Vector[\T, nat s\]` and `Matrix` are declared over `Array` when the nat fork lands and check shapes without changing storage.
132:Default: layered. It is the specification's own two factories (§5), the interpreter's own layering (§1), and it means this fork needs nothing from the nat fork to start and the nat fork changes no storage class when it lands.
133:
134:Why the default (unboxed, behind the generic, natives first, layered sizes), in one paragraph: it is the only path on which the first rung both compiles a microGPT-shaped kernel and puts a measured number beside the 6.3× (a `double[]` class with a native dot and product, timed against `KDotPrim`/`KMatPrim`), it changes no line of the model's text, it needs no change to the code generator to get its first number, it leaves the nat fork independent instead of blocking on it, and it follows the one precedent the team left in this world rather than a design they wrote for the other one.
135:
136:## 7. What happens right after the choice
137:
138:If (a): the failing test first, `library_tests/ArrayBoxed1.fss`, `a = array[\RR64\](4); a[0] := 1.5; println(a[0] + a[0])` printing `PASS` with a `.test` naming `link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=PASS`; verified to fail today at disambiguation on `Array`; then the boxed native class, its helper, the `NamingCzar` line, and `trait Array[\E,I\]` with `get`/`put`/`fill` in `CompilerLibrary`; full gate (a `.java` rung). Moves the ladder's 6 `Array` and 2 `array` files past disambiguation and microGPT's 8 `Array` components to the checker; `ImmutableArray`'s 26 wait for the immutable variant and `
139:
140:If (b): the failing test first, `library_tests/RR64Vector1.fss`, `v = makeRR64Vector(3); v[0] := 1.5; v[1] := 2.5; println(v[0] + v[1])`; then `FRR64Vector.java`, `simpleDoubleVector.java`, the trait, the two `NamingCzar` lines, the factory; full gate; in the same rung, kdot and kmat rewritten over `RR64Vector` with a native `dot` and product, timed against the Java baselines in `perf-probes/kernels/java/` (a measurement, not a gated test). Moves no ladder file and no microGPT component; the number is the deliverable.
141:
142:If (c), the default: the failing test first, `library_tests/ArrayRR64_1.fss`, `a: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = vec(4, fn (i) => 1.5 i); println(a[1] + a[2])`, with `vec` declared in the test's own component; then `trait Array[\E,I\]` with `get`/`put`/`|self|`, the `double[]` object `RR64Array1 extends Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` over `FRR64Vector.java` and `simpleDoubleVector.java`, the `NamingCzar` lines; full gate. Second rung, library only: `fill`, `map`, `ivmap`, the rank-2 object and `t()` as a view, with `kdot` compiled over a native `dot` and timed. Moves the ladder's 6 `Array` and 2 `array` files 
143:
144:Under every branch, the boxed default object for other element types, the immutable variant for `ImmutableArray`, and the compile path's overloading check on the model's operator pairs (§3) are the next three rungs, in whichever order the ladder counts and the model's needs rank them.
145:
146:## 8. The three probes behind §2 (2026-09-19, private cache, nothing committed)
147:
148:The compiler world's library was compiled into a private `FORTRESS_CACHES` in the order of `repo-internals.md:170-179` (five components, all exit 0), and each probe was `fortress compile` then `fortress run` from the scratchpad.
149:
150:Probe 1, stamping. `object Box[\T\](x: T) getter get(): T = x end` with `Box[\RR64\](1.5)` and `Box[\ZZ32\](3)`; prints `4.0` and `4`. The jar holds the template `GenBox$Box⟦⟧.class`, whose `javap -p` shows `Field "\%x":LT;` and `public T get()`. Run with `-Dfortress.bytecodes.expanded.directory` set, the loader saved the stamped `GenBox$Box⟦…FRR64⟧.class`, whose field is `Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64;` and whose `get` returns `FRR64`. A reference descriptor before and after; the stamped class's `RTTIc` carries a field `T` of type `RTTI`.
151:
152:Probe 2, element traffic on the unboxed vector. `v = makeZZ32Vector(4); v[0] := 3; x = v[0] + 1; println(x)`; prints `4`. `javap -c` of the program: `invokevirtual FZZ32Vector."[]"(FZZ32)FZZ32` then `checkcast FZZ32`; of `CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32Vector$DefaultTraitMethods.getValue`: `invokestatic native/…/simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, FZZ32)FZZ32`; of that generated wrapper in `nativewrapper_cache`: `FZZ32.getValue()I`, `simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, I)I`, `FZZ32.make(I)`.
153:

- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes (2026-10-20).** A demo that a change breaks is rewritten in the same batch where the way is known, as climb batch 20's rung I wrote a float base in three demos, `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB` and `BiCGSTAB2` and `10.0^(-6)` in `npbft`; one that fails for want of a feature runs again once the feature is built. His word of 2026-10-20 replaces his earlier "Let's not touch them", which likely came when a fix needed a feature not yet built. So the demos that fail today are respelled where the way is known: the five refused at load (row 670), `trips.fss` (row 710), `BiCGSTAB`'s timing line (row 791), and the static arguments a reduction needs under P-48 (row 731). Still to build: a measurement of which demos run, and a rung for those with a known way (PLAN, phase 3, item 19).
- P-80 **The sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset at run time.** The number chapters test a value's sign by comparison, and a float's finiteness by `check` or `check*` on `RR64`. `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex` stays word for word, marked superseded in the S1 form (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Built. Their return with covariance is P-62's.
- P-153 **An integer raised to a negative power raises an error; a fraction comes from a float or rational base (contract E, item 58).** Each integer type's `^` answers its own type at every exponent: a negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow` where the result is no integer, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code types an integer power by its integer at a signed exponent (P-26); overloads choose by type, and no type carries an exponent's or a numeral's sign, so the split is on the base, with the sign tested at run time as the library tests every sign-refined subset (P-80). Built in the one library and under walk. Still to build: the compiled path's own powers by the same contract, which answer 0 at a negative exponent today, when phase 4's natives bind the one library's `^` (rows 441 and 523; PLAN, phase 4, the natives).

### Arrays and the model program

- P-84 **Storage is `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes.** A high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So both are built together: sized types, the checker taught `nat` parameters, in the library's own patterns. How `double[]` goes under a float vector is array decision A (P-85).
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with array decisions A, B and D (PLAN item 13).** The three: a store per element type chosen by the factory, the size also kept as a field of the store, and a factory for a size known only at run time that returns the unsized `Array`. A is how `double[]` goes under a float vector, B where unboxed arithmetic happens, D sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is done before the switch-over. Array fork 3, on the third question's ground, is built at a default that waits for his review (review-queue item 30).
- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** An operator in the model never becomes a function call to satisfy an overload check. Any repair that changes a model line is shown to him as a diff before it is built. Decision D, the sized signatures of the flat program C4's vocabulary, is such a diff (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`); nothing of it is applied before PLAN phase 5.
- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** `Diag` extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, as the type system promises (row 299). A read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2` under `Array2`, is a library change for a later ledger row, not a vocabulary hack.
- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function (answer 10).** It is his answer to PLAN item 10. `fill` keeps the value form, every peer language's meaning of the word, and the function form takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Built; no model line changed.
- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked (PLAN, "Off the path, parked").
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main cost on microGPT's array kernels (F-11). Boxing is measured on microGPT-shaped kernels, not on a scalar loop with literals and a `:=` accumulator, which microGPT never runs. The storage is P-84's decision; unboxed arithmetic is PLAN phase 6 (P-33).

<!-- The design sketch for the first reserved fork of PLAN.md, the array representation on the compile path, written 2026-09-19 by a worker for Pavol and revised the same day after his three rulings (§6 quotes them): unboxed double[] is decided, the sized types are built as the team designed them with the checker taught nat parameters, and library work copies the library's own patterns. It assembles what next-climb.md §3a said a sketch must hold, adds the nat plan the second fork needs, and ends in a decision tree for what is still open. Eight probe programs were compiled in a private cache (§9); no tracked file was changed. Every recommendation is labelled "default" and decides nothing. One line per paragraph. -->

# How arrays should be built in the compiled world
Option (a), the interpreter's protocol ported boxed, is closed by Pavol's first ruling (§6) and is kept here only so the record shows what was rejected: about 1,200 lines of trait layer moved into `CompilerLibrary` over an `Object[]` native class; the fastest route to "the kernels compile"; the 6.3-6.5× kept; unboxing afterwards a second storage class under the same traits, "the same library written twice" (`map/README.md:127`).

### (b) `double[]`-backed arrays with unboxed elements designed in

What is built: `FRR64Vector.java` beside `FZZ32Vector.java`, the same 83 lines with `double[] val` and the four shape integers; `simpleDoubleVector.java` beside `simpleIntVector.java`; a trait in `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` with the nine members of `ZZ32Vector`; one line in `NamingCzar`'s special table and one in its foreign-route chain; a factory. That is the team's own five wiring sites. `ZZ32Vector` already covers the integer keys; `StringVector` the corpus.

Its own class, not a stamped instance: §2 verified that stamping substitutes class names into reference descriptors, so no instantiation of a generic template can hold a `double[]`; the `RR64` store is a hand-written class, as `FZZ32Vector` is, and anything reached through a generic trait's `get` is boxed at that boundary.

What the code generator must learn, if the loops are to run unboxed in generated code: an element read must become `getfield val:[D`, `iload i`, `daload` instead of the four-call chain of §2, and a bare `double` must have somewhere to go, which means a local variable slot of descriptor `D` and `dadd`/`dmul` for `RR64` arithmetic whenever the checker's static type is `RR64`, boxing only where a value meets a `T` or an `Any`. That is unboxing by static type (`performance-roadmap.md` A1) in `CodeGen.java` (6,750 lines) and `VarCodeGen`; every rung of it is a `.java` rung under the full gate with the 85 files as the net. Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured, and the Java model that would answer it is one more class in `perf-probes/kernels/java/`.

A second route to unboxed loops needs no code-generator change: write the loops of the vocabulary's operations as Java natives over `double[]` (the dot product, the matrix product, the elementwise maps, `SQRT`/`exp`/`log` over an array), so a box is paid once per whole-array operation instead of once per element. This is the shape of an APL implementation, each primitive a native loop, and microGPT in the C4 form is whole-array vocabulary; the residue is the user lambdas passed to `fill`, `map` and `rows`, which box per element. Not the team's precedent: their `ZZ32Vector` operators are Fortress loops over boxed subscripts (`CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535`).
